newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader says Mobutu must surrender.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader says Mobutu must surrender.

text.p: Frantic efforts to stage top- level negotiations to avert civil war reaching the Zaire capital suffered a setback on Friday when rebels demanded the unconditional surrender of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
At the same time, a rebel allegation, denied by Mobutu's camp, that the president had ordered a massacre of expatriates in Kinshasa to trigger foreign intervention sent a shockwave through the city.
Diplomats said they received worried calls overnight from their home capitals after the predictions of an impending massacre of foreigners were broadcast.
"It is clearly designed to spread panic in Kinhsasa and it is already succeeding in doing so," one Western diplomat said.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila hardened his tone over planned face-to-face talks with Mobutu, saying he would only attend a short ceremony on the transfer of power.
Kabila returned on Thursday to Zaire from exploratory talks in South Africa that raised hopes for a negotiated deal to halt six months of civil war.
On Friday he told Reuters by telephone from Zaire's second city Lubumbashi that his forces would march on Kinshasa if Mobutu declined to give up power.
"The South African initiative is about transfer of power. When he is ready for this, I shall go and attend a short day's ceremony on the peaceful transfer of power," he said.
"There will be no protracted negotiations with Mobutu, never, never. Maybe we have been misunderstood. The issue is about transfer of power otherwise we march on to Kinshasa," Kabila added.
Mobutu looked certain to reject the demand.
His security adviser and head of Kinshasa's negotiating team in South Africa, Honore Ngbanda, declined immediate comment on Kabila's latest remarks.
He told a news conference in Kinshasa that Mobutu had accepted on Friday South African President Nelson Mandela's invitation to meet Kabila.

Regional military sources told Reuters in Nairobi, Kenya, that Kabila's alliance -- already in control of about half the vast country -- appeared to be building up forces for an assault on Kinshasa should the veteran president refuse to go peacefully.
"They are preparing for an assault on Kinshasa should Mobutu refuse to go their desired way," said a source who closely monitors the six-months-old war.

South African deputy foreign affairs minister Aziz Pahad told a news conference in Cape Town on Thursday that Mandela had formally invited Mobutu to meet Kabila for talks and these would take place without preconditions set by either side.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga Mobutu, confirmed on Thursday that his 66-year-old father was now willing to meet Kabila but cast doubt on any prospect of Zaire's ruler of 32 years stepping aside.
Nzanga said Mobutu's departure would bring chaos to Zaire.
Kabila's bombshell remarks and the massacre plot charges were made at a time of heightened anxiety in Kinshasa.

U.S., French, Belgian and British forces based in the nearby Congo capital Brazzaville have stepped up training manoeuvres to prepare for an eventual evacuation of their nationals. About 1,500 Western troops are in Brazzaville.
U.S. Marines on Thursday staged elaborate manoeuvres with helicopters, with fellow marines playing the role of evacuees.
Kabila accused Mobutu through an aide of ordering the massacre of all expatriates in Kinshasa to provoke the intervention of the troops in Congo and avert his downfall.
In a statement to reporters in Lubumbashi Kabila sent the man he wants to be finance minister to give a warning that the alleged plot could "start at any minute".

"The AFDL (rebel alliance) has learned from very reliable sources that Mobutu and his team have charged his SARM (military intelligence) and DSP (presidential guard) to kill all the expatriates who live in Kinshasa," Mwana Nanga Mawanpanga said.
Nzanga dismissed the allegation as "ridiculous nonsense". "There's no foreigner here who will be killed by the government of Zaire, they are trying to spread panic," he told Reuters.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it suspended relief work for thousands of Rwandan Hutus in eastern Zaire on Friday after Zaireans attacked its staff in a protest over the presence of the unwanted refugees.

Spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said UNHCR wanted security guarantees from the rebels before resuming aid for more than 80,000 Rwandan Hutus after hundreds of protesters prevented an aid convoy from disembarking from a river ferry on the way to camps.
